chunks.content: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) in medicine has seen tremendous improvements in the past decade . Computer vision (CV), a subfield of AI defined as machine learning (ML) methods applied strictly to image inputs, has evolved rapidly with image classification and segmentation tasks achieving medical expert performance levels . Due to the advent of powerful computers, these models are able to train on large amounts of data and with new publicly available datasets, they have been growing rapidly . As a result, CV applications are being widely studied in medicine and are beginning to be used in clinical settings. The fields which have observed the largest impacts are those whose diagnostic tasks rely on pattern-recognition and have large amounts of images available. A prime example being radiology . However, CV applications are also being studied in other fields. For example, the delineation of cardiac structures and coronary arteries in cardiology , screening for diabetic retinopathy in fundus images in opthalmology , and detecting breast lesions on ultrasound in oncology . Considering that vascular surgery (VS) relies heavily on medical imaging for diagnosis, preoperative planning, and surgical guidance, it has important potential for CV implementation. Indeed, CV techniques have been studied for VS domains such as aortic, cerebrovascular, and peripheral artery disease. In Tomihama’s 2023 review of ML and image analysis in VS, the general CV approaches to abdominal aortic aneurysms and carotid artery stenosis were presented . From this review, it was made clear that despite significant research in this area, there is currently no paper synthesizing these efforts formally. As a result, there is much redundancy in this body of literature with several papers addressing common problems with similar approaches . Additionally, these have been found to use inconsistent metrics and do not adhere to standardized tools . Medical subspecialties have synthesized their CV efforts in an attempt to inform future research avenues. Current examples include Buyk’s 2023 neurosurgery and Kabir’s 2025 general medicine reviews . Furthermore, the Li 2022 systematic review synthesizes the use of ML in vascular surgery . However, as a result of its broad inclusion of various ML techniques, it is difficult to draw specific conclusions for CV applications from this study. Models built with structured data differ greatly from those trained on images in the types of architectures, training methodologies and performance metrics used. For the latter point, Li’s review compared study outcomes based on the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC): a widely used metric in ML models to assess the predictive capabilities of a binary output . However, such a metric would not be appropriate for a CV segmentation model. A dice score, which assesses the overlap of the predicted and true segmentations , would usually be the metric of choice. To this end, we conducted a systematic review and critical appraisal to formally synthesize the literature on CV applications in VS. Results Study Screening and Selection A total of 3924 unique studies were screened from MEDLINE ( n = 2154), Embase ( n = 2171), Cochrane CENTRAL ( n = 274) and Web of Science ( n = 1180) with duplicates identified by Covidence and manually. From title and abstract screening, 3182 studies were excluded and 742 were passed to full text screening. After this step, 288 were included for data collection and critical appraisal which included 46 studies from IEEE databases. From the full text screening, the majority of studies were excluded for not presenting a CV method (as defined in the Methods section) ( n = 374) or for not being VS related ( n = 45). This information is summarized as a PRISMA flowchart in Fig. and a complete list of all included studies is included in Supplementary Table and our Supplementary References. Inter-rater reliability (AL and JY) attained kappa scores of 84.9% for title and abstract screening and 78.3% for full-text screening. Study Characteristics The time trends, data sources, imaging modalities and CV architectures were studied for these papers. All of these characteristics are summarized in Fig. . In terms of the growth of this body of research, there has been an exponential rise as observed in Fig. A. Before 2017, there were only three papers: one from 2006 characterizing atherosclerotic plaque components in carotid arteries , another in 2013 detecting ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysms , and a study in 2016 measuring the intimal-medial thickness of carotid artery plaque . Since then, research in this field has greatly increased from two publications in 2017 to 75 in 2023 with a steady increase every year. Most studies (81.0%) used retrospective data to construct their datasets (Fig. B). Since then, research in this field has greatly increased from two publications in 2017 to 75 in 2023 with a steady increase every year. Most studies (81.0%) used retrospective data to construct their datasets (Fig. B). Of these papers, most collected data from their own institution (49.7%) or combined data from several centres (6.6%). Other studies used publicly available or shared datasets (24.7%) which was from data challenges, such as the international MICCAI challenge ; large publicly available datasets, such as the KAGGLE diabetic foot ulcer dataset ; or datasets requested from the studies of other institutions . A minority used prospective data sources (14.6%). Additionally, a small portion of papers simulated their data (2.1%) such as with the use of phantoms, which are models aimed to mirror human tissue biological characteristics . The five most prevalent publication countries for the included studies were China (28.1%), United States (16.3%), India (9.4%), Germany (6.6%) and France (4.2%). Almost all studies were retrospective cohort studies in nature (81.0%): none were case-control or cross-sectional. A minority of studies applied a prospective observational study design (16.7%). There were no randomized trials included. However, there was a single non-randomized clinical trial included in this review. This was an Italian non-randomized comparative clinical trial validating the performance of Wound viewer, a non-invasive, AI powered portable device, for wound evaluation. The study population consisted of 150 patients divided into three even groups: arterial and venous, diabetic and pressure ulcers. Images were taken with a specialized device that had a megapixel colour camera and several infrared sensors. These are then passed on to an algorithm based on a discrete time-cellular non-linear network that can segment wounds and, using colour scheme analysis, classify them. This group found that their device achieved 97% accuracy when compared to physician generated assessments of various wound characteristics, including area, depth, and proportion of granular and necrotic tissue, among other clinically relevant factors. Given these results, the authors concluded that Wound viewer is a reliable and accurate medical device for automated evaluation . The most common imaging modalities used for these CV applications were computed tomography (CT) (35.8%), with a spread of contrast and non-contrast images, and ultrasound (24.0%), including some video ultrasound as well (Fig. C). Other modalities used were conventional skin images (18.1%), thermograms (7.3%), magnetic resonance images (MRI) (8.0%), and X-rays (5.6%). Photoacoustic, laser speckle, multispectral and hyperspectral imaging were used in individual cases. Additionally, four studies (1.3%) implemented video based imaging modalities: three using video ultrasound for carotid plaque analysis – and a single study using endoscopic simulated videos to support automated guidewire control for endovascular surgery . The spread CV architectures are summarized in Fig. D. Convolutional neural networks (CNN) (27.4%), the base level architecture for image analysis , and U-Net (28.5%), a U-shaped CNN with added upsampling layers to improve local pattern recognition , were the most frequently used. For this CNN category, some studies used common architectures, such as YOLO , recurrent-CNNs , ResNet , Xception and VGG , while others created their own custom models. A few studies used commercially available softwares (2.8%) to train their CV models, such as ARVA , AtheroEdge , and AI-Rad , and others applied generative adversarial networks (GANs) (1.0%). However, the majority of studies applied a combination of several models (34.4%), either testing them separately or creating an ensemble with averaged predictions providing an output. In terms of general CV parameters, we recorded sample sizes but there was much variation in how this was presented. Some studies only considered the number of patients while others only provided the number of images. Overall, 257 studies recorded the number of patients with a mean of 153 and a range of [2-20,000] and 73 studies provided the number of images with a mean of 565 and a range of [12-61,190]. For training parameters, nearly all studies (83.3%) provided the train/test or train/test/validation split used. This refers to how the dataset was divided for the three portions of the algorithm. The most common splits (train/test) included 80/20 (22.6%), 90/10 (8.7%), 70/30 (5.6%) and 67/33 (3.8%). As seen from these splits, many studies did not include a validation dataset to evaluate for overfitting. Less than half (37.5%) of the studies provided a validation method for their training algorithm. The most common strategies were 5-fold (17.4%), 10-fold (7.3%), 4-fold (4.2%) and leave-one-out (3.1%) cross validation. These are all examples of k-fold cross validation: by combining the results of different train-test splits, this method allows for a better evaluation of model performance in an unbalanced dataset . As seen from these splits, many studies did not include a validation dataset to evaluate for overfitting. Less than half (37.5%) of the studies provided a validation method for their training algorithm. The most common strategies were 5-fold (17.4%), 10-fold (7.3%), 4-fold (4.2%) and leave-one-out (3.1%) cross validation. These are all examples of k-fold cross validation: by combining the results of different train-test splits, this method allows for a better evaluation of model performance in an unbalanced dataset . Nearly all studies applied offline processing methods whereby the model is trained in batches of data (99.3%). Online processing methods were found in only two studies, which involve real-time processing to update models continuously. One used active learning methods, whereby model predictions were corrected by reviewers and fed back into the training set . The second study compared online and offline methods for predicting AAA rupture status, with online models achieving superior outcomes . External validation, defined as testing on a separate dataset from input data, was performed in a minority of studies (10.4%). Explainability methods, which highlight important features in model decision making, were also infrequently used (14.2%) but the most common one was gradient class activation mapping (5.2%). Other methods used included shapley additive explanations , features maps or attention maps and these can all overlay heatmaps on images to illustrate what regions were most significant for predictions. Vascular Surgery Domains Certain areas of vascular surgery have observed much greater CV attention than others. Of the included studies, aortic disease (33.0%), carotid artery disease (29.9%) and foot ulcers (25.3%) were the most commonly studied (Fig. A). Some peripheral artery disease studies were present (6.2%) but the least common areas for CV applications included venous disease, visceral arterial disease, and lymphedema (all 0.7% each). Within the aortic disease CV studies, the most commonly studied areas were aortic aneurysms (35.8%) and aortic dissections (32.6%). For aortic aneurysms, papers focused on segmenting the aorta or aneurysm and some used a computational method afterwards to calculate the maximal diameter for diagnosis . Others attempted to segment parts of the aneurysm, splitting them into aortic lumen, thrombus, ulcerations , calcification and branches , or segmenting the aorta into distinct zones . A few studies tried to diagnose aneurysms or stratify their rupture risk directly from the CT image and used wall stress or pressure maps to make the diagnosis , . Two produced contrast-enhanced aortic aneurysm masks on non-constrast images using generative adversarial networks . This is an innovative solution to obtain contrast-like images without providing nephrotoxic solutions to a vascular patient population commonly co-diagnosed with kidney disease . On the other hand, for aortic dissections, most studies segmented the true lumen and false lumen of the dissections , , and occasionally segmented branches and thrombus as well . Others used CT images to diagnose the dissection directly and a few would further distinguish rupture from dissections or provide the Debakey classification . One study used bounding boxes to identify complications such as pleural effusions or poor renal perfusion . Similar to the aortic aneurysm study, one produced a contrast enhanced CT image of a dissection from non-contrast CT using a GAN. A large portion of studies also focused on endovascular aortic repair (16.8%) by segmenting endografts and predicting future endoleaks . Additionally, a group of aortic-related studies were not specific to a disease or procedure (13.7%): they either attempted to diagnose several diseases or segment and measure the aorta. As seen Fig. A, the majority of these studies focused on segmentation (58.9%) with few attempting to diagnose (16.8%) or provide measurements (15.8%) of these pathologies. CT images were by far the most frequently used imaging modality (85.3%). For carotid artery stenosis, several attempts to quantify the degree of stenosis with CV have been made. Segmentation was the focus of 74.4% of studies where most outlined the plaque itself or lumen-intima border and media-adventitia border in order to calculate the intimal-medial thickness , plaque area , degree of stenosis , or risk of rupture afterwards . Others characterized the tissue composition of the plaque: separating hemorrhage, calcifications, necrosis, fibrous tissue, or loose matrix . Some studies (18.6%) made these diagnoses directly: either classifying the tissue composition of plaque , providing a risk assessment of the stenosis , or predicting whether the patient is symptomatic . The vast majority of the studies used ultrasound (73.3%) but MRI (14.0%), CT (8.4%), and X-rays, including dental radiographs (3.5%), were chosen as well. Foot ulcer studies have been another major focus of CV applications in VS. The primary focus of this literature was diabetic foot ulcers but other types were considered as well. Foot ulcer studies have been another major focus of CV applications in VS. The primary focus of this literature was diabetic foot ulcers but other types were considered as well. The majority of studies (54.8%) were aimed at diagnosis . Variations included identifying ischemia or infection , or gangrene ; differentiating ulcers such as diabetic, pressure, surgical or venous ulcers ; or scoring according to the photographed wound assessment tool (PWAT) . Some studies (38.4%) also focused on delineating the wound boundaries . Only four studies made wound measurements such as length, width or area – . A single study attempted to use CV to synthesize wound images of venous leg ulcers using GAN in order to train future models . Skin images were most commonly used (68.5%) followed by thermography (27.4%), which makes use of the altered temperature distributions in foot soles with lower temperatures observed in ulcerated areas . Despite being a considerable fraction of a vascular surgeon’s clinical practice, peripheral artery disease (PAD) has seen very few CV applications (6.2%). These were either focused on segmenting the lumen of peripheral arteries (3.1%) and occasionally the occlusion as well, diagnosing PAD directly , or classifying the disease based on a scoring system such as GLASS , . Similarly, venous disease, as a separate entity from foot ulcers, is greatly underrepresented (0.7%) despite being another important aspect of VS practice. Performance Metrics Performance metrics provide a measure of similarity between CV model outputs and ground truths. Across all studies, there was considerable variation in the metrics chosen (Fig. ). The most frequently used were dice scores (51.3%), which considers the overlap of a prediction and ground truth making it ideal for segmentation tasks ; accuracy (36.5%), sensitivity (25.0%), specificity (15.0%), and precision (14.9%) which all consider true positive (TP), true negative (TN), false positive (FP) and false negative (FN) rates and combine them to reveal a unique characteristic of the prediction model; area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) (17.4%), which calculates the area of a FP vs. TP curve making it independent of any classification threshold ; and intersection over union (9.0%), which considers the areas of overlap and union in segmentation problems. For the metrics that were challenging to quantify and were therefore grouped in the “other” category, there was correlation coefficients (11.8%: kappa, overlap index, similarity), various error terms (11.1%: mean absolute error, mean squared error, median absolute difference, mean deviation), hausdorff distances (4.2%), time measures (3.1%: total performance time or percent time reduction relative to manual methods), negative predictive values (NPV) (1.0%), reliability (0.7%), and TP, FP, FN rates (0.4% for each). Risk of Bias and Critical Appraisal The PROBAST risk of bias assessment tool scores predictive models based on four domains: participants, predictors, outcomes and analysis. A low, unclear or high risk is assigned for each and an overall score can then be calculated. As observed in Fig. A, most studies did well in the predictors (98.3%) category. As these CV models used images as their predictors, the identification and explanation of the model inputs was straightforward. The studies scored well in the outcomes category with a low risk of bias rate of 67.7%. The chosen outcomes were consistently identified but some papers were deemed to have high risk for not explaining how the ground truths were chosen, failing to clarify which experts were making them, and not indicating whether any blinding process occurred. For participants, the studies performed adequately with half of the studies (49.7%) having a low risk of bias. Considering that most were retrospective, papers would be penalized for not specifying the inclusion period, the location of these patients or proper selection criteria. Additionally, for papers using challenge datasets, many did not provide an explanation of the study population (dates, location, selection criteria) and would only cite the paper associated with the dataset. However, the category which caused most studies to have high risk of bias was analysis: over half (57.6%) were deemed high risk. Although many studies did well to explain image preparation, they did not provide any hyperparameter optimization, failed to show any model training plots or an explanation of how overfitting was avoided (such as testing with an external validation dataset), did not incorporate a validation method, evaluated their main performance metrics on training data, or did not attempt to address the class imbalances of their datasets. An important concern is that a small portion of studies (6.6%) failed to provide a clear result for their model’s performance. TRIPOD+AI is a reporting standard specific to clinical prediction models using regression or ML methods. The performance across the various domains of this tool are provided in Fig. . Scores in the categories relating to the title, abstract, introduction and conclusion were high as was the data preparation and predictors domains. The acquisition of data (data and participants category), outcomes, overall analysis of model performance (analytical methods), and the inclusion of key acknowledgments at the end of the paper (ethics, funding, conflict of interest, registration) had some shortcomings. The acquisition of data and outcomes categories are similar to the participants and outcomes domains, respectively, from PROBAST and were penalized for similar reasons. The overall analysis looked at several aspects: studies performed well in model rationale, evaluation of model performance, predictors handling (such as transforms applied to the images prior to training), assessment of data heterogeneity and predictions calculations but lost points for measures and plots, and model updating. The high risk domains were related to sample size and missing data, failure to address class imbalances, not providing clear threshold values for model output, lack of a study protocol, no sections detailing data or code sharing or patient and public involvement, and failure to explain the steps in model development (such as hyperparameter optimization) and how model updating was tracked. Many of these subcategories align with the PROBAST analysis category and were penalized for similar reasons. Overall, adherence to the TRIPOD+AI guidelines was 56.5% averaged over all categories equally. Fairness was another key limitation in the studies, with only 19 (6.6%) providing a commentary on this issue. Some studies commented on their “racially homogeneous datasets” (Nomura 2023) which “often lacked meta-data including patient ethnicity, age, and sex” (Goyal 2020) as key limitations of their study. The source of imaging data was also identified as a key limitation since, ideally, it should be “collected from hospital systems using different machines and stored in different formats” (Long 2023) . However, in most cases, data was collected from few sources: one study cited that their “data [was] only collected from two medical centres...[which] could limit data diversity and affect the generalizability" (Dong 2024) . Of note, none of the included studies reported a formal fairness analysis of their models using direct covariates addressing the demographics of the dataset or indirect covariates regarding the imaging sources. As observed in Fig. C, although there has been some improvement in the quality of these studies, studies on CV in VS continue to be highly susceptible to bias. For the TRIPOD+AI adherence, calculated as the score averaged across all domains, it has increased from the low fifties before 2020 to over 60% in the most recent years. On the other hand, although there has been overall an improvement in the PROBAST risk of bias, the proportion of studies with low risk of bias remains low at less than 25%. Future Directions In the updated search between June 28, 2024 and January 7, 2026, 1631 new studies were identified and underwent title/abstract screening, with 197 passed onto full text review. The following study exclusions were made: 21 for not reporting a CV strategy, 16 for not being vascular surgery related, 9 for not being an original study or not providing results, and 6 manually-identified duplicates. Overall, 145 new studies were included. A complete list of included studies from the updated search is presented in Supplementary Table . Compared to previous results, most studies continued to address aortic pathologies (35.8%), with few focused on peripheral artery disease (4.8%). As seen previously, the most common imaging modalities included CT (42.0%), skin images (28.3%), and ultrasound (16.6%), primarily for aortic diseases, foot ulcers and carotid stenosis, respectively. Most studies continued to be retrospective in nature (93.8%). Dice coefficient (63.4%) and accuracy (40.0%) were the most commonly reported metrics, with AUROC present in a minority of studies (17.2%), as seen previously. Most studies continued to be retrospective in nature (93.8%). Dice coefficient (63.4%) and accuracy (40.0%) were the most commonly reported metrics, with AUROC present in a minority of studies (17.2%), as seen previously. With respect to critical appraisal, a significant portion of studies remained at high risk of bias (40.0%), with only 18.6% at low risk of bias. Studies expectedly performed well in the predictors category (99.3% low risk of bias). Studies were penalized in the outcomes category (81.4% low risk of bias), again primarily for not identifying how ground truths were chosen. Some studies did well in the participants category (44.8% low risk of bias) but were critiqued for not specifying the data source, inclusion period, or selection criteria. There was potential improvement in the analysis domain, with a decrease in the proportion of high risk of bias studies (57.6% -> 40.0%). More studies included model training plots and provided explanations for how overfitting was avoided, but this continued to be a common area for penalization. Furthermore, many studies continued to inappropriately evaluate performance metrics on training data. Discussion This systematic review aimed to capture the current state of CV research in VS. Our goal was to identify the performance standards of these models, the common methodologies that have been used, the limitations of their design and analysis, and the spread across VS domains. We found 288 studies with publications rising consistently since 2017. Much of this research has focused on three areas, aortic, carotid and foot ulcer disease, with significant under-representation of other domains that also rely heavily on imaging. Despite peripheral artery and venous disease making up a significant portion of VS practice, they have received far less attention from CV applications. Most studies were observational in nature and used retrospective data in the form of CT for aortic disease, US for carotid disease and skin images and thermograms for foot ulcers. U-net and other CNNs were the most standard models used but the majority of studies used several models to either compare their outputs or average their predictions. Less than half used a validation method, and very few studies tested their model on an external validation set or used an explainability method. These are not requirements but each of these components add more substance to a model’s prediction and can be considered essential components of a good analysis. The most commonly used metrics were dice scores, accuracy, sensitivity and AUROC. Finally, the risk of bias was high in 56.7% of studies, mainly due to shortcomings in their analysis, and adherence to reporting standards was low at 56.5%. Because of the strong dependence on imaging in VS, the exponential rise in CV focus for this field is a step in the right direction. Ideally, some of these research avenues can make their way into clinical practice to improve the efficiency of assessment and management of VS diseases. However, several limitations have been identified in this study: lack of prospective and external validation, disproportionate representation of VS domains, inconsistent performance metrics usage, and poor adherence to reporting standards. A major concern identified was the small number of CV studies in VS which included prospective evaluations. This limits our understanding of their real-world performance and likely hinders clinical adoption. Using retrospective data or public datasets to assess a model’s performance may not translate to results in a clinical setting. Despite the large number of efforts of CV in VS, there was only a single clinical trial included in our review. In order to incorporate these models into practice, studies should formally test their applications in prospective clinical trials, with a focus on demonstrating their potential to improve clinically relevant outcomes. On this note, the clinical trial that was included aimed to enable remote monitoring of foot ulcers and yet used a highly specialized device for their image acquisition . This may not be feasible to scale into virtual patient care compared to, for example, using a smartphone to take photos and having these uploaded to a cloud-based platform to diagnose the ulcers. This highlights the importance of clinical need driving these applications and how the design and development of these tools need to be centered around their use in clinical practice. Instead of a growing focus that has spread proportionately across the domains of VS, our results have identified that certain areas are saturated. Many studies have already attempted to diagnose and segment aortic aneurysms, aortic dissections, carotid artery stenosis and diabetic foot ulcers. Instead of a growing focus that has spread proportionately across the domains of VS, our results have identified that certain areas are saturated. Many studies have already attempted to diagnose and segment aortic aneurysms, aortic dissections, carotid artery stenosis and diabetic foot ulcers. They are, for the most part, using very similar CV models and training on the same imaging modalities. Although there is room for improvement in these models, they already have good performance in a research setting. For future avenues of research, we suggest focusing on other domains of VS. For instance, PAD takes up a significant portion of a vascular surgeon’s case load , often more so than carotid and aortic disease, and yet is starkly underrepresented in CV research. There is a known disparity in the amount of research and attention PAD garners relative to its incidence . Furthermore, PAD disproportionately impacts patients of racial minorities and lower socioeconomic status. Therefore, because PAD relies heavily on imaging for assessment and management and because of these known discrepancies , we strongly advocate for a larger focus of PAD in future CV endeavors in VS. From the included studies, there are few prognostic and diagnostic models for PAD. Prognosis may be an area of focus to consider: predicting the risk of disease progression from US and CT in order to guide medical management, follow-up and future surgical intervention. For diagnostic models, there are currently many anatomic classifications in PAD, such as TASC and GLASS . However, these are challenging to use routinely in clinical settings due to their complex and time-consuming nature. CV could be used to automate this classification to make them more clinically useful. These are all possible areas of future CV research in PAD that should be considered. Another interesting area of research to highlight is the use of CV to simulate contrast enhanced images. Considering that over half of VS patients have comorbid kidney disease , these models enable patients to avoid nephrotoxic contrast in these imaging modalities and endovascular interventions. However, the current state of research on this problem is limited with only three studies identified for aortic disease and one for general vascular disease (Supplementary Table ). Other imaging-reliant medical fields have been applying these techniques, especially radiology, with good performance – . GANs do seem to provide promising results with f1 scores of 0.85 and accuracies of 0.96 for VS diseases. This is an area for future research that improves clinically relevant factors. In terms of model performance metrics, our results highlighted a considerable variation in what was used. Comparison of performance metrics between studies is already hindered by testing on diverse, non-comparable, test datasets. It is therefore crucial to ensure that standard metrics are used to facilitate better comparability between studies. In terms of binary prediction models, despite a considerable number of our studies using these metrics, it is known that accuracy and sensitivity are poor markers of model performance and for this reason, AUROC is currently the reporting standard across ML . However, for clinical diagnostic problems specifically, this may not be a sufficient metric in isolation. Because of the importance of avoiding missed positive cases in medical settings, specificity, NPV and FN rates should ideally be included as well. On the other hand, for segmentation models, dice score is ubiquitously used in CV and, from our results, in VS as well. However, nearly half of the studies did not report a dice score or an AUROC (48.2%). In order to better compare the performance of these models, we strongly encourage the use of AUROC and dice score as the metrics of choice for discrimination and segmentation problems, respectively. Additionally, although a meta-analysis was beyond the scope of this systematic review due to study heterogeneity, future meta-analyses on this topic may benefit from funnel plots to assess for publication bias. As for technical aspects, few studies used external validation datasets which is an important aspect of the evaluation of model generalizability. If the model is too specific from over-training on input data, it will not generalize and will perform poorly on the external validation set. Because so few studies tested their models on external datasets, it is clear that most studies are not taking over-training into consideration. Although more resource intensive, online processing methods can simulate real-world applicability with models updated continuously. Only two of the included studies used such techniques, highlighting an area of improvement for future research. Additionally, explainability methods are for analyzing model predictions. It is a post-hoc method to determine what features of the input data were most associated with positive or negative predictions . Unlike structured

Because so few studies tested their models on external datasets, it is clear that most studies are not taking over-training into consideration. Although more resource intensive, online processing methods can simulate real-world applicability with models updated continuously. Only two of the included studies used such techniques, highlighting an area of improvement for future research. Additionally, explainability methods are for analyzing model predictions. It is a post-hoc method to determine what features of the input data were most associated with positive or negative predictions . Unlike structured data where classical statistics can identify correlations between specific variables and predicted outcomes, CV models can not rely on these methods. Therefore, explainability techniques provide an additional layer of substance to a CV model’s analysis by illustrating what the model is focusing on. However, only a fraction of the studies used such strategies. To improve the generalizability of the models and provide some form of rationale for their predictions, future research should incorporate both external validation sets and explainability methods. For a large portion of the studies, there were significant concerns around their methodologies. Overall, we suspect that this may be a result of the novelty of CV in VS with many new researchers testing these applications. Additionally, many of them may be unaware of PROBAST and TRIPOD+AI as these are relatively new (2019 and 2024, respectively). The improvement in the quality of studies over time suggests that they may be benefiting from new reporting standards and have shifted their understanding of ML as a black-box prediction tool to an algorithm requiring a sound methodology and proper justification. The growing attraction to CV has increased in recent years especially and this may explain the drop in PROBAST scores from new researchers once again entering the field. With early consultation of reporting standards, regardless of their CV experience, VS researchers can ensure high quality studies. Specifically, in terms of the PROBAST risk of bias assessment tool, we have identified that the majority of studies had shortcomings in their analysis. The greatest concern was around preventing overfitting: many papers were not providing training plots, not using a validation dataset, and not testing on an external set. Some studies evaluated their models on training data, which can significantly overestimate performance on real-world data. Overfitting can be a problem with any predictive model: if it is allowed to iterate over a training set in excess, it will become too specific to this dataset and consequently, will not generalize to other data . Outside of analysis, studies should properly identify the sources of their data, including a location and time period, and outline the process of creating ground truths. The latter point is especially important in CV applications where the ground truth may need to be created by trained professionals, such as for segmentation tasks. A clear process of how a group of medical experts were blinded to provide these ground truths are a necessity for these studies. We therefore strongly urge future researchers to consider these shortcomings in order to ensure they have properly identified their data source and process for ground truth generation and have a proper methodology to avoid overfitting such as evaluating performance on an independent validation, testing, or external dataset. Additionally, with the TRIPOD+AI 2024 reporting standards, many of the shortcomings identified with PROBAST were further elucidated. However, it also identified issues with class imbalances: studies were not making sufficient attempts to bridge the gap between event and control groups. As a result, the model may preferentially select for one over the other just based on the relative frequencies of the data being passed on to it. Studies also did not provide any fairness assessment of direct or indirect covariates: since demographic and imaging source factors influence the model’s training set, such methods should be used to ensure representative outcomes. Data sources were found to come from China or the US in nearly half (44.4%) of the studies, underscoring the potential lack of representation from lower income regions and the need for assessment of model bias and generalizability, as well as investment in developing CV algorithms using globally representative datasets. Additionally, many studies failed to provide an explanation of ethics, funding, conflict of interest or study registration. Although the nature of these CV studies may not seem to directly impact patients, there are still issues with privacy at hand and it is therefore important to clearly highlight this information. The study protocol was almost never provided despite being a crucial part of these research studies. Additionally, studies should make their data and code easily accessible to ensure that their results are reproducible and methodologies can be used by other researchers. The study protocol was almost never provided despite being a crucial part of these research studies. Additionally, studies should make their data and code easily accessible to ensure that their results are reproducible and methodologies can be used by other researchers. However, less than half of the studies provided these. An important limitation was the lack of patient and public involvement where nearly all studies overlooked this. Adding on to the earlier point of ensuring that clinical use is central when creating these CV applications, taking patient perspectives into consideration may help ensure that these tools are developed to improve relevant aspects of patient care. By following these reporting standards as early as during project brainstorming, many of these shortcomings can be avoided. The results from the updated search up to January 2026 underscored persistent shortcomings in this field. The main focus of CV applications in VS continue to be directed towards aortic disease, with less than 5% addressing peripheral artery disease despite it being a central aspect of VS practice. Most studies used similar CV techniques and imaging modalities. Nearly all studies were retrospective in nature, which may limit translation into clinical practice. Finally, although there were potential improvements, methodological shortcomings remain persistent, resulting in many high risk of bias studies. With respect to clinical translation, although these models show good performance in the research setting, several shortcomings have been highlighted: poor generalizability to real world datasets, lack of interpretability, high risk of bias and poor adherence to reporting standards. These issues limit the clinical adoption of these CV models. However, these problems are not unique to CV in VS and there are several commentaries suggesting how to appropriately address them. Firstly, studies should prospectively and externally validate their models to ensure their real-world applicability . Additionally, to improve clinician understanding and trust in model predictions, explainability methods should be applied to analyses . Finally, to ensure high quality reproducible models, researchers are urged to consult reporting standards, such as TRIPOD+AI, throughout their study. By implementing such strategies, CV models in VS can have greater potential for translation into clinical practice. This study has several limitations. Firstly, our study did not capture unpublished literature or perform citation tracking. Additionally, CV studies in VS may not consistently use relevant keywords in their abstracts and may not be consistently assigned to MeSH terms. Our use of textwords throughout our search strategy may have helped capture studies missed by MeSH terms. Additionally, although some non-English studies were captured by our search strategy, it did not account for language bias by including non-English keywords. Furthermore, given the time required for academic peer review and publication, systematic reviews on CV topics will likely need to be updated on a regular basis to capture the most recent developments in the field. PROBAST has not been validated in ML applications in the same way for predictive models, which is its main scope. Additionally, TRIPOD+AI was created for ML prediction models and may be less applicable to segmentation and generative models. As a result, many criteria are not as relevant, such as predictors, and others are not emphasized to enough of an extent, such as definitions of ground truth, for some of the CV applications. A key limitation reported in the CV literature is the lack of its unique guidelines. The current alternative that most studies use is the extrapolation of well-validated prediction guidelines, such as PROBAST and TRIPOD+AI . Future CV-specific guidelines may be helpful in guiding the development of these tools. In conclusion, we have conducted a systematic review and critical appraisal with 288 studies presenting a CV application for VS. Aortic, carotid and foot ulcer diseases have received the most attention in this field but PAD is underrepresented and should be a focus for future research. The use of a common metric, such as AUROC for discrimination and dice score for segmentation, will allow for better comparisons across these studies and future clinical trials should be encouraged to evaluate their performance in healthcare settings. Reporting standards, such as TRIPOD+AI 2024, should be consulted during the study protocol creation phase to ensure that ground truths are clearly established, methodologies adequately address over-fitting and other model engineering problems, that data and code is shared, and that the patient and public considerations are taken into account. Methods Protocol and Registration We conducted a systematic review that conforms to the PRISMA guidelines and this has been registered with the PROSPERO systematic review international registry (CRD42024555158). The PRISMA checklist is provided in Supplementary Note . As we only reviewed published articles and synthesized their data, ethical approval was not required. Search Strategy Our search strategy was created in consultation with an expert research librarian (AG). MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from inception to June 28, 2024. Of note, Web of Science includes IEEE database articles: a technical venue that captures novel state of the art models. All original studies on VS CV applications, defined as ML methods applied strictly to image inputs, on human subjects or models, were included. A combination of subject headings and keyword phrases were used to construct the search strategy. The general form of our searches was VS phrases, as a list of diseases or surgical procedures, which was intersected with CV phrases, as a list of CV or medical images with ML. Reviews, commentaries and studies on non-human models (animal-based data, etc.) were then excluded in the search. Studies on human-based phantoms were included. For papers not available in English, google translate was used. Our full search strategy is provided in Supplementary Table . Given the rapidly advancing nature of this field, an updated search was performed between June 28, 2024 and January 7, 2026, with the findings reported in a Future Directions section, understanding the need to continuously update knowledge synthesis to capture recent developments in VS CV applications. Study Selection and Data Collection Title and abstract screening, full text screening, data collection, and critical appraisal were performed by two independent reviewers (AL and JY) with a third author resolving discrepancies (BL). Covidence was used for uploading all papers and performing the study screening. All studies that presented a CV application of VS were included provided that they were applied to human models, were not reviews or commentaries, and had full texts available. Studies using other mathematical algorithms, such as active contours, gray level covariance matrices, energy optimization, or classical radiomics, were excluded for not meeting our definition of a CV application. For data extraction, a standardized data collection form was created and all included studies were exported from Covidence. Covidence provided the DOI, title, year published, authors and journal name. The other data columns included the clinical objective (segmentation, diagnosis, measurement, etc.), vascular disease or procedure, data source (retrospective, data challenge, etc.), inclusion period for retrospective studies, ground truth, image type (X-ray, etc.), output prediction, sample size, event size, CV architecture, use of an explainability piece for the model, validation method, training split, outcomes and metrics, and use of an external validation dataset. PROBAST risk assessment tool was used for the critical appraisal with low, unclear or high risk of bias selected for the participants, predictors, outcomes and analysis sections. From these scores, an overall risk of bias score is calculated for each study as indicated by the PROBAST guidelines . Additionally, we scored every study according to the 2024 TRIPOD+AI guidelines with a binary variable used to assess all of its domains . Data Analysis The data from the collection sheet was transferred to a Python 3.9 Jupyter Notebook for data analysis. For all major analysis domains, key phrases and recorded data were grouped into major categories and the number of instances in each group were calculated to provide counts or divided by the total number of studies to provide frequencies. Since a meta-analysis was beyond the scope of this systematic review, the outcomes across studies were not synthesized. No missing data strategies were required and no heterogeneity or sensitivity analyses were performed. Introduction Medical Device Related Pressure Injury (MDRPI) is a pressure injury (PI) caused by sustained contact of a medical device with the skin or subcutaneous tissues, resulting in impaired blood circulation, which in turn causes tissue ischemia, hypoxia, and necrosis ( ). MDRPI is one of the common complications in surgical patients, especially in prolonged surgeries ( ). PI not only increase patient pain, prolong hospitalization and increase healthcare costs ( ), but also may lead to serious complications such as infection and sepsis, which can endanger the patient’s life ( ). Respiratory devices, including endotracheal tubes, often have MDRPIs ( , , ). The technique of transnasal tracheal intubation is widely used in oral cavity, head and neck surgery because it provides the surgeon with a better view of the operation ( ). As a specialized dental hospital, which is common procedure used the transnasal tracheal intubation technique. During prolonged procedures, the transnasal tracheal tube exerts continuous pressure on the nasal skin and mucosa, which in turn causes ischemic and hypoxic damage to the nasal tissues and predisposes to transnasal tracheal tube-related nasal PI ( , ). In recent years, the incidence of malignant tumors of the oral cavity, head and neck has continued to rise, and related surgeries have increased year after year, with prolonged surgical times and an increased incidence of nasal PI ( , ). Nasal PI not only affects the patient’s facial aesthetics that cannot be easily repaired ( ) and increases the patient’s pain and treatment costs, but may also prolong hospitalization and affect the patient’s recovery and prognosis. Routine nursing measures, such as the use of hydrocolloid dressings or modified methods of tracheal tube fixation, although effective in preventing nasal PI ( , ), still have limitations in prolonged surgery. Furthermore, the incidence of PI is of concern to all levels of healthcare as a sensitive indicator of quality of care ( ). Therefore, hospitals pay special attention to the important topic of preventing the occurrence of nasal PI. In recent years, the Multidisciplinary Collaboration Model (MCM) has not only gained widespread use and recognition in the medical field, but also plays an important role in the prevention of stress injuries ( ). By integrating the expertise and skills of different disciplines, it is possible to assess risk more comprehensively and develop targeted interventions. Under the auspices of the hospital’s Patient Safety Initiative, in 2024 we undertook a special improvement activity for the prevention of intraoperative transnasal tracheal tube-related nasal pressure injuries in a multidisciplinary collaborative model. Materials and methods This is a single-center, historical controlled study to investigate the clinical effectiveness of implementing a multidisciplinary collaborative model for the prevention of transnasal airway catheter-related nasal PI in patients undergoing prolonged oral, head and neck surgery as a special quality improvement activity in a municipal dental specialty hospital in China. The historical control group, which received routine preventive measures, was compared with the intervention group, which received a multidisciplinary, collaborative, whole process prevention and control strategy. We hypothesized that effective prevention of nasal PIs in patients undergoing prolonged surgery and transnasal endotracheal intubation requires the implementation of a multidisciplinary collaborative model and improvement of prevention strategies. This special improvement activity was carried out in 2024 at the Affilated Stomatological Hospital of Chongqing Medical University, People’s Republic of China. This hospital is a major municipal hospital specialized in oral and maxillofacial surgery. The operating room is the main site of the study. The sample for this study was determined from the chart review based on the inclusion exclusion criteria. The sample was selected from surgical patients who underwent elective oral, head and neck surgeries between January 2023 and December 2024 at the hospital. The historical control group was identified through chart review; between January and December 2023, the hospital used routine care measures for nasal PI prevention and control, and 221 surgical patients who met the inclusion and exclusion criteria were selected as a sample. The intervention group was identified as 294 surgical patients who met the inclusion exclusion criteria as a sample of 294 surgical patients who met the inclusion exclusion criteria during the period of January to December 2024, when the hospital implemented a total nasal PI prevention and control strategy in a multidisciplinary collaborative model. This study was a retrospective analysis designed to assess the effectiveness of implementing quality improvement activities to reduce the incidence of nasal PI in 2024. In 2023, 221 patients were enrolled, of whom 16 had nasal PI (7.24% incidence); in 2024, 294 patients were enrolled, of whom 7 had nasal PI (2.38% incidence), for a total sample size of 515. This study was a retrospective analysis designed to assess the effectiveness of implementing quality improvement activities to reduce the incidence of nasal PI in 2024. In 2023, 221 patients were enrolled, of whom 16 had nasal PI (7.24% incidence); in 2024, 294 patients were enrolled, of whom 7 had nasal PI (2.38% incidence), for a total sample size of 515. The sample size was calculated for the comparison of two independent proportions using a two-sided significance level of 0.05 and a target power of 80%. Based on historical quality surveillance data from 2023, the incidence of nasal pressure injury was estimated at 7.24%. For this quality improvement initiative, a clinically meaningful and achievable reduction to approximately 2.0% was prespecified. Allowing for unequal group sizes consistent with the study periods, the minimum required sample size was approximately 194 patients in the control group and 257 in the intervention group. The final sample (221 vs. 294; total 515) exceeded this requirement. Inclusion criteria for the historical control group and the post-implementation intervention group: ① surgery time ≥3 h; ② age ≥18 years; ③ BMI of 18.5–23.9 kg/m 2 ; ④ transnasal tracheal intubation. Exclusion criteria for the historical control and post-implementation intervention groups: ① preoperative comorbid diabetes mellitus or severe malnutrition or uncontrolled hypertension; ② preoperative nasal skin or mucous membrane injury, infection, or history of previous nasal surgery; ③ preoperative coagulation dysfunction or use of therapeutic doses of anticoagulant medications; and ④ emergency surgery or loss of visitation within 24 h of the operation, which prevented nasal evaluation. The multidisciplinary collaborative nasal PI prevention and control strategy was developed in January 2024 with the support of the hospital’s Patient Safety Initiative. The multidisciplinary team consists of medical administrators, nursing administrative personnel, anesthesiologists, surgeons, wound therapists, and operating room nurses. The team members receive PI-specific training ( ) to ensure that each member has the relevant knowledge and skills, and then work together to implement a full process prevention and control strategy that consists of a structured, comprehensive, and dynamic risk assessment—a dynamic graded intervention—and a structured post-operative follow-up visit. Medical administrators and nursing administrative personnel work together to develop prevention and control strategies and monitor the quality of implementation. Wound therapists perform PI risk assessments preoperatively and postoperatively using the Braden Risk Assessment Form, and structured return visits were performed within 24 h postoperatively for nasal skin status. Operating room nurses performed dynamic PI risk assessments and implemented graded interventions using the modified Competency, Outcomes, and Resources in Nursing (CORN) scale to assess the risk of nasal pressure injuries preoperatively, intraoperatively, and postoperatively. Nasal skin assessments were conducted immediately after extubation and at 24 h postoperatively. While most acute nasal injuries are visible within this timeframe, it is noted that this follow-up period primarily focuses on the immediate impact of the medical device during the perioperative phase. Anesthesiologists, surgeons, and operating room nurses dynamically adjusted the graded interventions according to the risk level, including: selecting an appropriate thickness of tracheal tube and lubricating it adequately before anesthesia, applying eye ointment or petroleum jelly or Sai Botanic Lotion to the skin in contact with the nose of the nasotracheal tube ( , , ); wrapping the nasotracheal tube, the filter, and the respiratory tubing and their connections with a disposable transparent and aseptic protective sleeve before surgery; maintaining optimal suture tension—secure enough to prevent tube dislodgment but sufficiently loose to avoid mechanical tissue compression during surgery; and removing the sutures in time after the operation. Paying attention to the skin of the nose during the operation, and adjusting the position of the transnasal endotracheal tube visually in real time so that the endotracheal tube hangs as far as possible in the nasal cavity. The “mobile nursing system” functioned as a decision-support tool, automatically triggered prompts based on real-time CORN scores: Preoperative nursing interventions: low risk: routine lubrication and standard fixation. Medium risk: use of eye ointment/petroleum jelly/Sai Botanic Lotion at contact points; wrap nasotracheal tube (NTT), filters, etc., with laparoscopic camera sleeve. Intraoperative nursing interventions: low risk: monitor nasal skin condition. Medium risk: remind surgeon about appropriate suture tension for nasal/NTT fixation; adjust NTT position; remind surgeon not to suture-fix NG tube to NTT and to remove promptly post-op; keep NTT suspended in nasal cavity as much as possible. High risk: all medium-risk measures plus apply eye ointment, moisturizer, or povidone-iodine to nasal area during wound closure. The key to this quality improvement activity is multidisciplinary collaboration and division of labor to complete assessments and implement precise interventions. Therefore, prior to the start of the improvement activity, a one-week special training was conducted for team members, with each member participating in at least two training sessions and simulation exercises, and an assessment was conducted to ensure that 100% of the team members mastered the use of the assessment forms and the correct implementation of the interventions. The multidisciplinary team utilized a modified CORN scale for dynamic risk assessment (see for the full scale). To ensure inter-rater reliability, all assessors underwent simulation training, achieving a Kappa coefficient of 0.85 before the study began. These assessments followed the standard staging criteria (NPUAP) with all diagnosed cases cross-checked by a second independent senior nurse to reduce observer bias. The protocol for this study was approved by the Ethics Committee of The Affiliated Stomatological Hospital of Chongqing Medical University (no. 2025 Clinical Review [037]). Since this study was a retrospective analysis of clinical data collected during a quality improvement project (2023–2024), the Ethics Committee granted retrospective approval. Statistical analysis The relevant data for 2023 and 2024 were extracted into Excel spreadsheets through the hospital’s Madison surgical anesthesia system, and mobile care system, respectively. The principal investigator reviewed the medical record data based on inclusion and exclusion criteria. Surgical patients were compared one year before and after the implementation of this quality improvement activity. The incidence of nasal PI was the outcome metric of the study. This indicator directly reflects the effectiveness of the intervention and facilitates comparison of the effectiveness of the intervention between the two groups, the historical control group (before the quality improvement activity was implemented) and the intervention group (after the quality improvement activity was implemented). Data for both groups were extracted through chart review. Basic patient data, including age, gender, height, and weight, were collected through the Madison Anesthesia Clinical Information System, as well as surgery-related data, including type of surgery, anesthesia modality, anesthesia start time, and surgery end time. Data related to the patient’s health status were collected through the mobile nursing system, including the presence of preoperative comorbidities of diabetes mellitus, severe malnutrition, and uncontrolled hypertension; preoperative nasal skin or mucosal injuries, infections, and history of previous nasal surgery; preoperative coagulation dysfunction and use of therapeutic doses of anticoagulant medications; and the occurrence of intraoperative nasal PI. To minimize the inherent bias associated with a historical control design, we ensured that the clinical environment remained consistent throughout the study period (2023–2024). Specifically, there were no significant changes in the composition of the anesthesia teams, the nurse-to-patient staffing ratios in the operating rooms, or the standard intraoperative temperature management protocols. All surgical procedures were performed using identical models of nasotracheal tube and medical equipment across both groups. Furthermore, the postoperative care pathways followed a unified standard operating procedure (SOP), ensuring that the observed differences in nasal pressure injury (PI) rates were primarily attributable to the multidisciplinary intervention rather than external co-interventions or secular trends. Discussion Nasal pressure injury is one of the common complications in patients undergoing transnasal endotracheal intubation, which is mainly due to local tissue ischemia and hypoxic injury caused by continuous direct pressure ( ) exerted on the nasal skin and mucosa by the transnasal endotracheal tube and its attached filters and respiratory threaded tubing. Although routine nursing measures, such as nasal application of hydrocolloid dressings or modified methods of tracheal tube immobilization ( , , ) are effective in preventing nasal PI, they have significant limitations in dealing with the complex scenarios of prolonged surgery. These routine care measures make it difficult to achieve dynamic redistribution of pressure, much less effectively reconcile the conflicting demands of anesthetic operations (e.g., catheter fixation stability and ventilation safety) with the demands of surgical procedures (consistently optimized exposure of the operative field). Therefore, for such high-risk surgical patients, there is an urgent need for a systematic prevention and control strategy that goes beyond a single nursing perspective, and a systematic prevention and control system can only be constructed through the integration of anesthesia, nursing, surgery, and wound management and the adoption of a multidisciplinary collaboration model. In this study, a special quality improvement program relying on a multidisciplinary collaborative model was successfully implemented with the support of a special patient safety initiative in a Chinese municipal dental specialty hospital. At the heart of the project is the formation of a collaborative team that integrates the professional strengths of medical administration, nursing administration, anesthesiology, surgery, wound care, and operating room nursing. Through the implementation of the whole-process prevention and control strategy of “structured and comprehensive dynamic risk assessment—dynamic graded nursing intervention—postoperative structured return visit”, the incidence of nasal pressure injuries associated with nasotracheal tube was significantly reduced from 7.24% in the historical control group to 2.38% in the intervention group, and the occurrence of serious injuries of stage 2 and above was effectively eliminated. This remarkable result strongly confirms the superiority of the multidisciplinary collaboration model in solving complex clinical problems and improving patient safety and quality. The successful implementation of this project relies on the synergy of a number of key strategies, two of which stand out as constituting the core innovation of the study: The most groundbreaking innovation of this study is the preoperative use of a disposable transparent sterile protective sleeve to completely wrap the transnasal endotracheal tube, filter, and respiratory threaded tubing and their connection sites. Compared with the improvement of using 2 sterile cloth towels for wrapping, this technique offers three significant advantages: on the one hand, the weight of the wrapping material exerts direct pressure on the nose through the transnasal airway tube, and compared with 2 sterile cloth towels (approximately 175-250 g), a single disposable clear protective sleeve weighs approximately 24 g, which significantly reduces direct pressure on the nose through the transnasal airway tube over a prolonged period of time. On the other hand, we focus on the regular readjustment of the position of the transnasal airway tube. The disposable transparent sterile protective cover provides an unobstructed and clear view, which enables the operating room nurses to directly and real-time observe the specific pressure point of the transnasal airway tube on the nasal tissues during the operation, and combined with the results of the dynamic risk assessment, the team was able to timely and accurately adjust the position of the transnasal airway tube on the nose, and to achieve the dynamic redistribution of pressure ( ), which fundamentally improves the disadvantages of the traditional fixation, which is difficult to adjust or requires “blind” adjustment. Furthermore, while optimizing the pressure adjustment, the disposable transparent sterile protective sleeve tightly ensures the sterile barrier and physical tightness of the respiratory line connection, completely eliminating the risk of accidental disconnection or contamination of the line that may be triggered by intraoperative adjustment operations, thus fundamentally safeguarding the patient’s ventilation safety. This innovation cleverly resolves the tension between the need for pressure redistribution and the safety and security of breathing lines, which is often difficult to reconcile in conventional methods. The supporting core strategy is the construction of a dynamic assessment and graded intervention system that is structured and managed throughout the process. The system employs a dual system of risk assessment: an overall pressure injury (PI) risk assessment of the patient by the wound therapist using the Braden Risk Assessment Scale preoperatively and postoperatively; meanwhile, the OR nurse performs a dynamic, specialized risk assessment using the modified CORN Intraoperative Acquired PI Risk Assessment Scale preoperatively, intraoperatively, and postoperatively. The key innovation of the Modified CORN Intraoperative Acquired PI Risk Assessment Scale is the embedded specifics of graded interventions that correspond to the risk level assessed in real time. The system employs a dual system of risk assessment: an overall pressure injury (PI) risk assessment of the patient by the wound therapist using the Braden Risk Assessment Scale preoperatively and postoperatively; meanwhile, the OR nurse performs a dynamic, specialized risk assessment using the modified CORN Intraoperative Acquired PI Risk Assessment Scale preoperatively, intraoperatively, and postoperatively. The key innovation of the Modified CORN Intraoperative Acquired PI Risk Assessment Scale is the embedded specifics of graded interventions that correspond to the risk level assessed in real time. The mobile nursing system automatically triggers and prompts graded interventions corresponding to the corresponding risk level based on the risk level assessed in real time, which greatly enhances the timeliness and accuracy of the team’s response and ensures that medium- and high-risk patients are provided with more timely and accurate preventive measures, an innovation that further realizes information technology-driven precision interventions. In terms of interventions, a multi-component “combo” has been developed: At the source control level, the anesthesiologist selects a catheter of appropriate thickness based on the patient’s anatomy and lubricates it adequately, and preapplies eye ointment, petroleum jelly, or Sai Botanical Lubricant to reduce friction at the site where the catheter comes into contact with the nose ( , , ), and then uses the same type of fixation tape and the same type of fixation; During the intraoperative dynamic maintenance session, the surgeon is responsible for fine-tuning the tightness of the nasal fixation sutures and ensuring that they are removed in a timely manner, while the operating room nurse performs the aforementioned visual catheter adjustments and makes every effort to ensure that the endotracheal tube remains as “airborne” as possible within the nasal cavity in order to minimize direct pressure on the nasal tissues. Finally, a structured post-operative visit within 24 h to assess the condition of the nasal skin creates a closed loop of “assessment-intervention-feedback” to ensure early identification and management of any potential problems. The key to the success of the multidisciplinary collaboration model is the establishment of a clear division of specialization and an efficient synergy mechanism: Leadership and quality control. In this quality improvement activity, experts from the Department of Medical Affairs and the Department of Nursing worked together to develop a framework of prevention and control strategies and quality control standards based on evidence-based rationale ( , ), organized regular quality analysis meetings, monitored the implementation process and promoted continuous improvement, and provided key organizational safeguards and professional guidance, which were critical to the success of the project ( ). Professional technical implementation, including anesthesiologists leading the selection of transnasal tracheal catheter model ( ), lubrication and provide positional adjustment of professional advice and security; maxillofacial surgeons accurately regulate the tightness of the patient’s nasal fixed sutures, timely removal of sutures; The wound therapist conducts PI risk assessment, provides professional guidance on skin protection, leads the development and application of PI science videos and picture books for preoperative education, and enhances the knowledge of doctors and patients about PI; The operating room nurse, as the implementer and coordinator, is responsible for performing dynamic preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative assessments using the modified CORN Intraoperative Acquired Pressure Injury Risk Assessment Scale, implementing graded interventions, performing visual catheter adjustments, monitoring nasal conditions in real time, and performing structured return visits within 24 h of surgery to ensure that potential problems are detected and addressed early. The multidisciplinary collaboration model breaks down disciplinary barriers and promotes information sharing and resource integration. A week-long special training and simulation exercise ensured that 100% of the team members mastered the assessment tools and intervention process. Regular interdisciplinary exchange meetings and trainings have effectively brokendown professional barriers, facilitated the sharing of expertise and integration of experience, and developed and standardized actionable operational standards for nasal PI, which not only enhances the relevance and effectiveness of interventions, but also reduces duplication of efforts and waste of resources. The results of this study suggest that a dedicated quality improvement campaign in a multidisciplinary collaborative model with an integrated strategy of combining multiple preventive measures significantly reduces the incidence of nasal PI associated with transnasal tracheal catheters. This finding is highly consistent with existing relevant international literature emphasizing the effectiveness of multidisciplinary collaboration and comprehensive prevention strategies. For example, studies by Guido Ciprandi et al. ( ), Delmore et al. ( ), and Pittman et al. ( ) point to the fact that the proper application of comprehensive prevention strategies by interdisciplinary teams can be effective in preventing the occurrence of stress injuries. Studies by Gupta et al. ( ), Chaboyer et al. ( ), and Gaspar et al. consistent with existing relevant international literature emphasizing the effectiveness of multidisciplinary collaboration and comprehensive prevention strategies. For example, studies by Guido Ciprandi et al. ( ), Delmore et al. ( ), and Pittman et al. ( ) point to the fact that the proper application of comprehensive prevention strategies by interdisciplinary teams can be effective in preventing the occurrence of stress injuries. Studies by Gupta et al. ( ), Chaboyer et al. ( ), and Gaspar et al. ( ) have also demonstrated that multidisciplinary teams can significantly reduce the incidence of stress injuries through PI risk assessment and proper implementation of a range of preventive measures. The unique value and contribution of this study is: Technological innovation. For the first time, we have proposed and practiced the use of disposable transparent sterile protective sleeve for visual catheter adjustment technology, which provides an innovative solution for realizing dynamic redistribution of pressure during operation and guaranteeing the safety of respiratory line, especially suitable for oral head and neck surgery with high requirements for both the operation field and the safety of ventilation. Specialized hospital application verification. For the first time, the effectiveness of the multidisciplinary collaborative whole-process prevention and control model for nasal PI associated with transnasal tracheal tube has been systematically constructed and validated in the specific scenario of a municipal dental specialty hospital in China, providing a practical template that can be borrowed by similar specialty institutions. Structured process and information technology empowerment. A clear structured assessment-intervention-monitoring-return-visit process has been established, and through the combination of the improved CORN intraoperative acquired stress injury assessment scale with embedded intervention prompts and the mobile nursing system, a rapid and precise translation of risk assessment results to interventions has been realized, enhancing process efficiency. Patient experience enhancement. Patients spoke highly of the systematic and refined care under the multidisciplinary collaboration model, believing that it not only improved the quality of care, but also enhanced their sense of security and trust in medical services, helping to improve the doctor-patient relationship and enhance the hospital’s reputation. Despite the positive outcomes, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, this study utilized a single-center, historical controlled design, which is inherently susceptible to secular trends and temporal confounding. While we have adjusted for key factors such as age, BMI, and surgery duration, other variables like subtle shifts in surgical case-mix or anesthesia staffing over time might influence the outcomes. However, given that our department maintained stable staffing and standardized perioperative protocols during the study timeframe, the impact of these variables is likely minimal. Future prospective randomized controlled trials are needed to further validate these findings. Second, the follow-up duration for nasal pressure injuries was limited to 24 h post-operation. Existing literature suggests that some medical device-related pressure injuries may fully manifest within 48 to 72 h. Therefore, our study may have underestimated the true cumulative incidence of late-evolving injuries. However, given that the majority of transnasal tubes in this study were removed shortly after surgery, the 24-h assessment captured the peak period of direct device-related stress. Future research should implement longer monitoring windows to capture the full progression of these injuries. Third, the modified CORN scale, while integrated into our mobile nursing system for real-time prompts, was used as a site-specific assessment tool for nasal injuries. Its specificity and predictive validity for this particular anatomical site require further validation and optimization through prospective studies with larger, multi-center cohorts. Finally, as this quality improvement project was conducted in a specialized dental hospital focusing on oral, head, and neck surgeries, the findings may not be directly generalizable to other surgical specialties or different clinical environments. Future research should employ multicenter, prospective, or stepped-wedge cluster randomized designs to confirm the long-term clinical and cost-effectiveness of this multidisciplinary collaborative model. Conclusion This study amply demonstrates that a multidisciplinary collaborative model of specialized quality improvement activities for the prevention of nasal pressure injuries associated with transnasal tracheal catheters in a specialized municipal dental hospital. By breaking down professional barriers, integrating technical resources, and constructing a closed-loop management system of “assessment-intervention-monitoring-return visit,” the incidence of nasal PI associated with transnasal tracheal catheters in patients undergoing prolonged surgery of the oral cavity, head and neck can be significantly and effectively reduced, and the occurrence of serious injuries of Stage 2 and above can be effectively prevented. This successful practice not only significantly improves quality of care sensitivity indicators, enhances patient safety and experience, provides new ideas and methods for nasal PI prevention, but also provides a replicable and scalable systematic solution for the prevention of such complications in similar specialized medical institutions.
